# What changes now {#sec-ch22}

::: {.epigraph by="William Gibson, attributed"}
The future is already here. It's just not very evenly distributed.
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
from jevkit.econ import TASK, task_cost
```

We started this book with a question a lot of people are asking right now:

*"Do I really need to learn all of this?"*

You've learned quite a lot of it since. Probability and calibration, neural networks, embeddings, attention, LLMs, agents. Then a new kind of model, and everything it takes to use one well. This last chapter is shorter. It steps back and asks what all of that adds up to, for the industry and for you.

I'll try to be careful here. It's easy to end a book like this with predictions, and most predictions about AI age badly. So I'll stick to three things: what the book showed, what it suggests, and what nobody knows yet.

::: {.goals}
- See the decision layer as its own layer in an AI system, separate from generation.
- Estimate what moving decisions out of an LLM changes for one of your own tasks.
- Know which skills become more valuable when decisions get cheap.
- Keep an honest list of what isn't known yet.
- Leave with a plan for your first three months.
:::

## A layer of its own

For the last few years, the default design for an AI system has been one big model doing everything. It reads the input, decides what to do, writes the output and calls the tools, all as text.

![Two ways to build an AI system. Left: one model does everything as text. Right: each layer does one job. An LLM reads and writes, a decision layer answers typed questions with probabilities, a policy turns those into actions, and tools, logs and people sit underneath.](/figures/ch29/stack.pdf){#fig-stack}

The right-hand side of @fig-stack is the shape this book kept arriving at, chapter after chapter. The LLM does what only an LLM can do: read anything, and write for people. The decision layer answers small typed questions in one pass, with probabilities you can test. The policy draws the lines, from costs and capacity. And underneath, tools act and people review.

Each layer is smaller than the system it serves. Each can be tested on its own, with the tools from Part I. And each can be replaced without rebuilding the others: a better LLM, a different decision model, new lines. That, more than any benchmark, is why I think the split will last.

## What gets cheap

Take one task, sketched the way Chapter 7 counted Kestrel's agent: a ticket comes in, an agent picks tools, checks whether it has enough, checks whether an action is safe, does it and writes a reply.

::: {.tryit lab="ch22"}
```{python}
decisions = sum(n for _, kind, n in TASK if kind == "decide")
steps = sum(n for _, _, n in TASK)
print(f"{decisions} of {steps} steps are decisions")
for who in ("llm", "jev"):
    s, d = task_cost(who)
    print(f"{who:>4} decides: {s:4.1f} s and ${d * 1000:.2f} per 1,000 tasks")
```
:::

![One illustrative agent task, with its decisions made by an LLM or by a decision model. The writing step costs the same either way; the decisions are where the difference is.](/figures/ch29/task.pdf){#fig-task}

With the book's illustrative LLM figures and Jev's vendor-reported ones, the task drops from about {{< num ch29 task_llm_s int >}} seconds to {{< num ch29 task_jev_s int >}}, and the bill falls by about three quarters (@fig-task). What's left is mostly the one step where an LLM writes something a person will read. Chapter 17 measured the same shape on Kestrel's agent, which ran about {{< num ch29 ch24_speedup int >}} times faster as a hybrid.

Then Chapter 12's warning applies. When decisions get this cheap, we won't make the same decisions for less. We'll make many more of them: every login checked, every retrieved passage judged, every agent step gated. Most of the change will happen there. It won't come from doing today's work more cheaply. It'll come from the work that becomes worth doing.

## What gets valuable

If deciding gets cheap, what becomes scarce?

Judgement about the decision itself. Someone still has to decide what a mistake costs, where the lines go, how much the review queue can take, and whether the probabilities are still honest this week. The model can't do any of that for you.

![Skills that matter more when decisions get cheap, and skills that matter less on their own, with the chapters that teach each.](/figures/ch29/skills.pdf){#fig-skills}

Which is why the book's first part, which may have felt like a long detour, was worth the time. Thinking in probabilities and testing calibration were the foundations, not the preamble (@fig-skills). They're what separates a system that makes a million cheap decisions well from one that makes a million cheap mistakes.

What matters less *on its own* is prompting for everything, and reaching for the biggest model by default. Both still have their place. They're just no longer all of it.

## What nobody knows yet

I've tried throughout to keep three piles: what's verified, what's vendor-reported and what's unknown. @fig-unknowns is the unknown pile, as it stands.

![Open questions, and what you can do about each today.](/figures/ch29/unknowns.pdf){#fig-unknowns}

Every item in @fig-unknowns is open. None of them is a reason to wait. Calibration on your data is a test you can run this week. Drift between versions is a pin and a monitor. Prices are a spreadsheet with a sensitivity column. And the question of who else builds decision models matters less than it seems, because the pattern outlives any vendor. A typed question in, a probability out, and a policy in your own code: you can move that to a different model on a Tuesday afternoon.

::: {.keyidea}
You don't need to predict how this plays out. You need decisions you can measure, lines you can move and a model you can swap.
:::

## What to do on Monday

![A first three months, one decision at a time.](/figures/ch29/monday.pdf){#fig-monday}

If you do one thing after closing this book, make it the audit in the first box of @fig-monday. List every decision your system makes, and count them. Most people are surprised by how many there are, and by how many are small, typed and frequent. The lab for this chapter is a template for that.

Then pick *one*. Get a few hundred labels. Test it the way Chapter 11 did. Put prices on its mistakes, draw its lines and run it in shadow. Switch it on with a fail-safe and a monitor. Then do the next one.

It isn't glamorous. It's how every system in this book got better.

::: {.breaks}
This chapter is the most speculative in the book. The cost and speed figures are illustrative, and Jev's are vendor-reported from its early access. The claim that a decision layer will become a standard part of AI systems is my reading of the evidence here, not a finding. It could be wrong if general-purpose models become fast and well calibrated enough that splitting stops paying off. If that happens, the skills in @fig-skills still apply; only the box they live in changes.
:::

::: {.threshold}
Your own system: pick the decision in it that happens most often. What does a wrong "yes" cost? A wrong "no"? Where does the line go? And how would you know, a month from now, whether the probabilities behind it are still honest?

(There's no answer at the back of the book for this one. If you can fill in all four, you've learned what this book set out to teach.)
:::

::: {.bookquote by="Alan Turing, Computing Machinery and Intelligence, 1950"}
We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done.
:::

Turing ended his most famous paper with that sentence [@turing1950]. It fits this moment well.

3. Pick one item from @fig-unknowns and design the smallest test that would move it into the "verified" pile for your use.
